I have concluded for the moment all that I wish to say with respect to the speech from the throne, but before I resume my seat I should like to say a word or two with respect to one or two matters that are in the minds of hon. members and which are conspicuous by the absence of any reference to them in the speech from the throne. It will be realized that in what I said this afternoon there has been constant reference to the fact that the government has proceeded, in practically everything it has done, as if it were an executive wholly independent of the House of Commons, rather than an executive which derives its powers from and is responsible to the House of Commons. Indeed, the House of Commons has come to be, in the phrase used by the Prime Minister himself not so long ago, a sort of rubber stamp for what the ministry may choose to do, regardless of how its own wishes and desires may be expressed, and regardless of how much those wishes and desires may represent the wishes and desires of the people at large.
In 1919 this House of Commons approved of an address to His Majesty the King praying that His Majesty should thereafter refrain from conferring titles and titular distinctions upon Canadians or persons ordinarily resident in Canada, and in accordance with this expressed wish of the house an address was presented to His Majesty. The resolution approving that address has stood upon the records unamended, unqualified, unchanged in any particular, it has not been rescinded; it is there to-day, and I believe from the time it was passed until practically the concluding hours of last session, every government, every parliament, every hon. member of both houses of parliament believed that resolution to be binding upon the ministry of the day. But at the conclusion of last session, the Prime Minister made in the house a surprise announcement with respect to the resolution which gave, not the opinion of the law officers of the crown or of the House of Commons, but his own opinion on the matter, which was to the effect that the resolution was not valid, and had no legal effect. Since that time the Prime Minister himself has recommended to His Majesty the conferring of certain titular distinctions and titles upon certain Canadians, and he has done

so in defiance of the resolution as passed by the House of Commons.
In speaking on this subject I wish in the first instance, to make clear that I am not at this time going to discuss the merits of titles in themselves. This is not the time to discuss that phase of the subject. There is on the order paper a resolution which relates to the question of titles, and when that resolution comes to be discussed will be the time to debate the merits of the question. But this is the proper time to discuss the rights of and privileges of this House of Commons in respect to resolutions which it may pass and the extent to which such resolution may be binding upon the ministry.
Let me make clear one other point. In what I am about to say in this debate, I have no intention of in any way discussing the royal prerogative, beyond considering how the prerogative with respect to honours is to be exercised in the conferring of titles on His Majesty's subjects in this country. The question of the prerogative is not at issue at all. The royal prerogative is unquestioned. The question at issue is the conditions under which and the advice upon which the royal prerogative is to be exercised in this dominion, and that is the essence of the resolution which was passed by this house. It was in reality a direction to the ministry of the day as to how the commons, as representing the people of this country, believed it should exercise its power with respect to the advice to be tendered to His Majesty in the exercise of the royal prerogative as respects the conferring of titles on Canadians.
Perhaps it will facilitate debate on the matter and help to make clear just how definite and strong the trend of opinion has been, if I say a word or two about the way in which the prerogative with respect to titles has been exercised in Canada in the last fifty or sixty years. From the time of confederation down to 1902, I think one may say, the question of how titles were to be conferred, by whom the recommendation was to be made to His Majesty, was one that was more or less undefined. That I think is the simplest way in which to state the matter. There were at all events two points of view. One which I think I may say has since been wholly discarded, but which was held by the British government, was that, with respect to titles, it was the duty of the Colonial Secretary to make the recommendation to His Majesty. The Colonial Secretary in making his recommendation might do so entirely on his own initiative, getting his information from such sources as he thought best, or he might do so

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
more directly on the recommendation of the Governor General sometimes in consultation with, sometimes without consultation with, the Prime Minister. So far however, as the Prime Minister or the ministry of the day was concerned, until 1902 neither figured very largely in the mind of the British Government as having any real control in the granting of titles.
In 1902 the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier passed an order, in council which was communicated to Mr. Joseph Chamberlain, then Secretary of State for the Colonies, and in which the government set out what it believed to be the correct practice with respect to conferring titles upon Canadians domiciled in Canada. For the purpose of accuracy I shall quote from the communication two or three paragraphs which I think are of special significance. Before doing so however, there is one other point which at the moment I should like to make clear in connection with this discussion.
In speaking of titles in this debate, I am referring only to such titles as were taken cognizance of by the resolution of 1919. That is the only resolution which is before us for consideration; it is the one instruction binding upon the ministry in addition to the orders in council that bear upon the subject. The resolution of 1919 was quite specific in certain directions. It did not touch certain classes of recognition at all; in fact certain classes of recognition were specially exempted. It made no reference whatever to titles that appertain to an office, titles in the nature of professional or vocational appellations; it left those to one side. The committee which dealt with the matter and which made to the house the recommendation upon which the resolution was based, had considered, for example, the question of the title of "right honourable" as applied to a member of the Imperial Privy Council, and the title of "honourable" as applied to members of the government. It decided that those particular titles or designations should not be included in the address to be sent to His Majesty, and they, therefore, do not enter into the present discussion at all. So far as decorations are concerned, I have not any desire to bring into this debate the question of what are commonly called decorations.
The feeling against titles in this country is I think directed against one particular style, of title, namely, that which carries with it the prefix "Sir" before the Christian name of the person on whom the title is conferred, and, by courtesy, the title "Lady" before the name of the wife of the recipient of such an
honour, thereby serving to set up in this country an exclusive social class. There is where the main, in the case of many the whole, objection to titles in Canada arises: it helps to create a class which, in virtue of the manner in which its members are to be addressed by their fellow citizens, are set apart in the dominion, as a separate, exclusive class of knights and ladies. The feeling in a democratic country like Canada is very strong against that sort of thing, and that feeling has found expression in this House of Commons many years in succession, and concretely in the resolution to which I have referred. It is to that class of title I am referring. There is no necessity to refer to hereditary titles; I think that matter has been definitely settled, but the survival here of the old feudal order of knighthood, given to certain chosen individuals nominated at the instance of the Prime Minister, and which cannot be ordinarily supported without a certain amount of wealth is the kind of thing of which the people of this country want as little as possible.
I should now like to read part of the text of the order in council passed by the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier on February 19, 1902. The paragraphs that are significant are as follows:
On a report dated February 15, 1902, from the Right Honourable the Prime Minister submitting that the exercise of the royal prerogative conferring honours and titular distinctions upon His Majesty's subjects in Canada is one which has not hitherto been brought into harmony with the principles of parliamentary government, of which it is an important part.
The Prime Minister further submits that the great development of Canada, and the high position which she has now obtained, render it advisable that upon this subject, as upon all others, the exercise of the royal prerogative shall conform to the well understood principles of ministerial responsibility.
There, as long ago as 1902, in an order in council which is still of record and in the files of the council, emphasis was laid upon bringing this whole matter into harmony with the principles of parliamentary government. Do the principles of parliamentary government permit of a ministry doing what it pleases notwithstanding the known will of the members of the House of Commons, as expressed by them, no matter what justification it may find or seek to find from other sources? Is there conformity with the well understood principles of ministerial responsibility when the ministry, at a time when parliament is not in session, does a thing which without the House of Commons altering a decision which it had previously reached by way of instructions to the ministry it would hesitate to do

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
and could not and would not do, were parliament in session? I mention these points because they have stood from 1902 to the present time. This is 1934; we are talking about custom and tradition and the rights of the commons. This affects every hon. member who has a seat in this house; it affects his right and privilege as a member of parliament whose constituents have strong feelings on these matters, to have his rights and privileges protected against any ministry or any prime minister. The order in council goes on to say:
The Prime Minister states that in practice, since the establishment of confederation the granting of honours and titular distinctions upon the subjects of the crown in Canada has been the result of correspondence between His Excellency the Governor General and the colonial office, and of recommendations made by the former, usually yet not invariably after consultation with the Prime Minister but not in conformity with any settled principle and without constitutional responsibility.
The practice is not in harmony with the principles of our constitutional system.
There again the same note is being emphasized. Then a little further down the order goes on:
The Prime Minister submits that while His Majesty may take the initiative in respect to the bestowal of honours and titular distinctions the minister should be none the less responsible for what may be - done. To the ministers of His Majesty at Westminster responsibility attaches for every reward conferred for public service within their sphere of action. In Canada a government similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom has been established, and the advisers of His Majesty in Canada are the proper advisers of His Majesty for every kind of reward bestowed upon His Majesty's subjects for services performed within the legal and constitutional sphere of Canadian jurisdiction.
I direct attention to those words because the Prime Minister himself, speaking to this House of Commons towards the close of last session, presented the view that His Majesty was free to confer honours on his own initiative, that such was a part of his prerogative. I say that while that may be a part of the prerogative of His Majesty in the old coimtry, thought that I do not admit for a minute so long as this, and another order in council to which I shall refer a little later stand, in Canada the prerogative cannot be exercised by His Majesty on his own initiative. His Majesty's prerogative with respect to the granting of titles in Canada is restricted by this order in council, which is part of the law of the land, and which sets forth the necessity of that prerogative being exercised on the advice of his ministers. Let me read the words again, because I think probably 
we will find that the leader of the government may take issue with them:
The Prime Minister submits that while His Majesty may take the initiative in respect to the bestowal of honours and titular distinctions the minister should be none the less responsible for what may be done.
It can only be on the responsibility of a ministry, and of the Prime Minister in particular, that so far as Canada is concerned, the prerogative may be exercised. The concluding portion of the order is as follows:
-and respectfully ask that the royal instructions be modified to the effect that the same rules which apply for the exercise of the royal prerogative in granting honours and titular distinctions to subjects of the king in the United Kingdom be made likewise to apply to all recommendations by the Governor General for the exercise of the prerogative to the king's subjects in the colonies, and that all such recommendations by the Governor General to the sovereign in such matters be made upon the advice of his responsible ministers.
One would have thought that the order in council would have met with immediate acceptance in the old land, but that was not so. The British government of that day and particularly Mr. Joseph Chamberlain, took the position that it was not for the Canadian government to say what should be done, but that, the Secretary of State for the Colonies, with respect to imperial orders such as that of St. Michael and St. George should make recommendations to His Majesty; that with respect to distinctions which concerned science, literature and the like, the Governor General should form his opinion and communicate with the Secretary of State for the Colonies; but that, in regard to political honours, the Prime Minister or the government of the day might of course take the responsibility of making recommendations.
I need not stop to read further from the despatch from Mr. Chamberlain, as I have outlined its main features. To some extent the matter rested at that point for a number of years. Evidently, Sir Wilfrid Laurier did not wish to be involved in a controversy; I think he was fortunate in being associated with governors general who were very like himself in their desire to work in harmony in all matters, and I believe he had no difficulty on the score of agreeing with the Governor General of the day in the matter of such recommendations as were made.
. The next important stage in the consideration of this subject was in 1918. In that year the question came up because His Majesty did confer certain distinctions which proved to be most unpopular, whether or not on the advice of the Canadian government, I am not

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
in a position to say. At any rate honours were conferred which served to arouse feeling, particularly as they were of a hereditary character; and the House of Commons concerned itself with the matter.
I want to direct the attention of the house immediately to this point, that, whenever in these discussions the question has come up for consideration in parliament it has come up in the House of Commons. It is not a matter which has greatly concerned the other house of parliament, it is one which is primarily the concern of the House of Commons. This House of Commons is the body to which the ministry is responsible, and in all matters relating to the exercise of the prerogatives of the crown it is the House of Commons which asserts its rights in terms of how the prerogative is to be exercised.
In 1918 Mr. Nickle of Kingston introduced a resolution, seconded by Mr. McMaster, to the effect that all hereditary titles should be abolished. An amendment to the resolution was moved by Mr. Richardson of Lisgar to the effect that no titles should be granted. Sir Robert Borden, who was leading the Conservative party and the government of the day, stated to the house that a short time previously the government had considered the matter and had passed an order in council in connection therewith, which had been transmitted to the British government. He said that, inasmuch as his government had set forth its position with respect to titles, he felt that the House of Commons should take no further action in the matter at that session, especially in view of the fact that there was to be a conference in England that year which he, Sir Robert, would attend and upon which occasion the whole matter would be discussed with the British government. He gave the assurance to the House of Commons that, if the matter were allowed to stand over for another year, he would see to it that at least in that year no titles of any kind would be conferred. He carried out his promise to the extent of declining even to recommend decorations during that time, although there was nothing in the resolution or in the discussion which had touched that phase of the matter.
The order in council which Sir Robert brought down is a very important document. From it I should like to quote two or three paragraphs, because I believe they make very clear Sir Robert Borden's views. He indicated that he was dealing with a matter of concern not merely to the House of Commons but to the whole country, and that the purpose was to direct the ministry with respect to the exercise of the prerogative and
not in any way to seek to restrict the prerogative of the crown, as such. The order in council is dated March 25, 1918, and is as follows:
The committee of the privy council have had under consideration a report dated March 9, 1918, from the right hon. Prime Minister touching the procedure for conferring titles of honour upon subjects of His Majesty ordinarily resident in Canada.
Submitting that the subject demands consideration and attention, the Prime Minister observes that the royal prerogative of conferring honours and titular distinctions for important public services is unquestioned, but that it is necessary to consider the conditions under which and the advice upon which it should be exercised within this dominion.
I ask hon. members to note those words. That is in the order in council which remains and governs the present ministry. The order is to-day part of the law of this country.

It has the
authority of a government of which the minister was a member. It is a policy which he endorsed and approved. I am directing the attention of the house to the view as expressed by the leader of the then Conservative party, who was in office at the time, and I am outlining its contention as to how titular distinctions should be dealt with. Let me continue:
It is necessary to consider discussions under which and advice upon which it should be exercised within this dominion. He submits that the bestowal of honours is a matter of concern to the whole community and has a direct relation to the orderly government of the state.
There, Mr. Speaker, is a clause to which I wish to direct the attention of the house. The government of Sir Robert Borden solemnly declared, and the Prime Minister speaking for the government and for himself declared, that the bestowal of honours is a matter of concern to the whole community. I wonder if the Prime Minister of to-day will deny that such is the case. He certainly denied it when parliament was not in session; in the face of the resolution which was passed in 1919, he recommended to His Majesty the creation of certain titles. I submit that this House of Commons, representing the community, is entitled to very special consideration of any matter which a Conservative Prime Minister has said he regards as a matter of concern to the whole community. To continue reading:
Having regard to the firmly established principles of self-government in Canada the Prime Minister is of opinion that no title of honour or titular distinction should hereafter be conferred upon any subject of His Majesty ordinarily resident in Canada except upon the direct advice and responsibility of His Majesty's Canadian government. Such an assumption of control by the government of Canada follows the natural course of constitutional development in this country as the tendency has invariably been in the direction of complete control of every function of government.
In the light of the Prime Minister's apparent belief that such is not the case and that, so far as Canada is concerned, His Majesty is free, on his own initiative, to make recommendations or appointment, I submit that, from the point of view of constitutional practice and procedure and of methods which have governed in the past and still govern in connection with the exercise of this prerogative, it can be exercised in Canada only in the

manner indicated in the passage I have read from Sir Robert Borden's order. Let me read one further statement:
The Prime Minister is not aware of any other prerogative of the crown which in its relation to Canada is not exercised on the advice of His Majesty's Canadian ministers and he is unable to agree that a different principle should be maintained in the exercise of the prerogative of conferring honours.
There is the following statement in the substantive part of the order:
No honour or titular distinction saving those granted in recognition of military services during the present war or ordinarily bestowed by the sovereign proprio motu shall be conferred upon a subject of His Majesty ordinarily resident in Canada except with the _ approval or upon the advice of the Prime Minister of Canada. The government of the United Kingdom shall exercise the same authority as heretofore in determining the character and number of titles or honours to be allocated to Canada from time to time.
I believe the last clause will be regarded as out of date now, in view of the fact that we have the statute of Westminster governing in matters of this kind. The point I wish to make clear, however, is that at the time the matter was under discussion, Sir Robert Borden and his ministry made it perfectly clear that the question of titles is one affecting the whole community and for that reason one of special concern to the House of Commons ; and that the ministry could constitutionally and properly make recommendations only in the light of what it knew distinctly to be the expressed wish of the House of Commons.
That was the position in 1918. In 1919 the subject was again discussed. In the meantime Sir Robert Borden had visited England; in fact, he was in England at the time. In 1919, a new resolution was brought in, again by Mr. Nickle, this time recommending that no titles of any kind should be recommended. An amendment was proposed to that resolution to the effect that some provision should be made with respect to hereditary titles in this country which would prevent their being continued upon the death of the then holder. In the absence of Sir Robert Borden, Sir Thomas White, who was then leading the government, suggested the appointment of a special committee of the House of Commons to inquire into the whole matter and to make a recommendation to the house. A special committee was appointed which made its recommendation and it was the recommendation of that committee which was endorsed by the resolution passed in 1919. I shall read just a paragraph from that resolution:

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the House of Commons of Canada, in parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty, praying that Your Majesty may be graciously pleased:-
(a)	To refrain hereafter from conferring any title of honour or titular distinction upon any of your subjects domiciled or ordinarily resident in Canada save such appellations as are of a professional or vocational character or which appertain to an office.
(b)	To provide that appropriate action be taken by legislation or otherwise to ensure the extinction of an hereditary title.
The committee in its report says:
A suggestion was made that the titles of "right honourable" and "honourable" be discontinued, but the suggestion did not meet with the approval of the committee.
The committee in its report also went on to say:
Your committee, however, do not recommend the discontinuance of the practice of awarding military or naval decorations, such as the Victoria Cross, Military Medal, Military Cross, Conspicuous Service Cross, and similar decorations to persons in military or naval services of Canada for exceptional valour and devotion to duty.
That is the substance of the resolution of 1919. That resolution clearly was taken by the government of the day and by all subsequent governments to bind the ministry. As I have said, that resolution was not a resolution which could affect the prerogative of the crown as such. The prerogative remained as it was, and as it is to-day, and) as it will continue; but what it did affect was the powers of the ministry in advising His Majesty how that prerogative should be exercised.
Just to show the house how completely public opinion as expressed in this House of Commons has been opposed to any restoration of titles, I might recall that in 1923, on March 19, Mr. Ladner, one of the Conservative membei-s in the house of that day, introduced a resolution which would have permitted decorations-not titles, but simply decorations-to be given in recognition of services in literature, art or science. That resolution was negatived by a vote of 121 to 14, indicating very clearly what the House of Commons of that day felt about any attempt to reintroduce titles even by this seemingly innocent means.
In 1929 the present hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) introduced a resolution in the house which showed very clearly, so far as he was concerned, that he believed the government of the day to be bound by the 1919 resolution of the House of Commons, and he sought to have that resolution qualified or
amended or rescinded. I think those words were carefully chosen, and I must say that I like very much the form in which my hon. friend introduced his motion. I think he went the right way about it. That was in 1929, ten years after the resolution of 1919 had been passed. My hon. friend the present Secretary of State, at that time sitting on this side, asked the house to appoint a committee to consider whether the resolution of 1919 should not be qualified, amended or rescinded. As Prime Minister of the day I had to take a . position with regard to my hon. friend's resolution. I tried to give him as open a door as I could to get the matter considered. I believed that any committee that dealt with the matter would reach the decision that the resolution of 1919 should stand, but, nevertheless, I was glad to have a committee appointed, if the house were willing to appoint it, and I so stated. I said that I did not think the matter should be made a party issue in any sense of the word, but that members should be free to vote as they pleased, and I supported my hon. friend's motion. True enough the hon. member from North Huron (Mr. Spotton) sought to have the impression conveyed that, in even allowing a motion for a committee to investigate the matter as Prime Minister at the time, I was favourable to titles. However, Mr. Dunning, the then Minister of Railways, made quite clear that the government itself, if it had to take a stand in the matter, would oppose titles, but that some of its members were prepared to have a committee of the house consider the matter if the house itself was willing to have its own committee look into it. My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) says to me not to include him, that he voted against the appointment of that committee.
Let me now read the resolution of the present Secretary of State as it was moved in this House on February 12, 1929:
That a special committee of this house consisting of eleven members be appointed forthwith, to investigate and report upon the advisability of qualifying, amending or rescinding the address to His Majesty the King, which was adopted by this house in May, 1919, dealing with the conferring by His Majesty of titles of honour or titular distinctions upon His Majesty's subjects domiciled or ordinarily resident in Canada; and also to consider and report upon the appropriate action, if any, which the parliament of Canada should take with respect to the acceptance, enjoyment or use by persons domiciled or ordinarily resident in Canada of titles of honour or titular distinctions or decorations conferred by any foreign government, governmental authority, potentate or power; and also to consider and report upon the advisability of instituting orders of merit,

distinctions or decorations, which may be conferred by His Majesty upon persons domiciled or ordinarily resident in Canada, on the advice of the government of Canada, in recognition of distinguished public services; and that such committee have power to send for persons, papers and records, and to report from time to time to this house.
That was the resolution of my hon. friend (Mr. Cahan), a very modest and, as I have said, an excellently drawn resolution. How did the house receive that motion? It negatived the motion by 114 to 60. The house would not even permit the consideration of the question of qualifying or amending the resolution of 1919. My hon. friend the Secretary of State to-day is a member of the government which is responsible for having recommended to His Majesty the giving of titles to one or two gentlemen, notwithstanding that his belief in 1929 clearly was that the resolution of 1919 was binding upon the government of the day.
I fail to see any inconsistency whatever.

More than that, the Prime Minister himself was in the house at that time, and if one reads the debates one will not find in anything the Prime Minister then said the ground he is alleging to-day for recommendation being made by the ministry to the sovereign. He himself accepted the view of the house as it was held at that time. So it is quite clear that, from the time that resolution of 1919 was passed, right down until the last session of parliament everyone believed that the resolution of 1919 was binding upon the ministry.
Now what took place last session? It is interesting to note that this matter was not brought up in the first session, or the second or the third or in the fourth session of this parliament until its very end; the government waited until almost its last chance had arrived, to take any action in the matter. What was done in the last session? As will be recalled, my right hon. friend from Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) had received a promotion in the honours list of the previous New Year. He had been a Knight Commander of the Order of St. Michael and St. George, and he was made a Knight Grand Commander. That was an innocent sort of thing, and I must say that all of us who are so fond of him were pleased to see him get the promotion. But I think it would have been much finer if he had waited to receive it until after the House of Commons had rescinded the old resolution and then to have obtained it by going in through the front door instead of by one at the back.

Shortly after the house resumed in the New Year, a question was put upon the order paper by the hon. member for Laurier-Outremont (Mr. Mercier) asking, among other things, whether this promotion meant that we were to have titles restored.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There was another one associated with it.

As my right hon. friend says, some reference was made also to other honours which had been conferred upon certain individuals, I think by His Holiness, the Pope. As far as this country is concerned we have no state church, and, so far as honours conferred by any church are concerned, they lie altogether outside the control of the House of Commons or the ministry. There is no established church and the country does not receive nuncios.
Might I remind my hon. leader of one thing? If these promotions came through the back door they were put at the front door by being published on the first page of the statute book of last year.

The exact date the question was asked is of small importance, but my recollection is that it was some time in January or February. However, it was well on in the month of May-right at the end of the session-before the question was answered. To the surprise of everyone, the Prime Minister in making reply made the statement that he did not regard the resolution of 1919 as binding upon the ministry in any way, that it was a resolution of a House of Commons in one parliament and did not bind subsequent parliaments. That is at best questionable. I notice that May, speaking of resolutions, says that some resolutions are held to bind subsequent parliaments although passed by one only; that the matter is more or less one of custom. So far as custom is concerned, it certainly had become the custom here to hold that the resolution was binding. The Prime Minister knew that hon. members felt strongly on the subject either one way or the other, and I think he must have known that they would wish to express themselves with respect to the matter in an open and straightforward way before any action should be taken by the ministry. He made that statement, and as was my duty in following parliamentary practice, I asked the Prime Minister if in view of the lateness of the session, he would not see to it that the government did not

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
make any recommendations to His Majesty between the close of that session and the opening of the present session. It is perfectly true that the Prime Minister replied that he would give no such assurance. That was characteristic of the sort of reply which he makes to most of the questions I put to him; I took it as such and I think most hon. members thought the same. I was not speaking for the opposition alone; I was speaking for hon. members on his side as well as hon. members on this side who wished to be given an assurance in this regard. I do not think any hon. member thought that before parliament re-assembled the Prime Minister would take action contrary to the letter and spirit of the resolution. At that time he told us that the time was too short to hope to discuss the matter at that session. If that was the case, surely there was good reason to wait until this session before taking any action. There the matter rested.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Prime Minister did not object to any motion of censure or otherwise being moved by the opposition.
That sounds very well.

speechtext: No, he did not.
As my right hon. friend well knows, it was only ten days before the close of the session and at that time we of the opposition were doing what we could to help to shorten the session.
Oh, oh.

We were doing what we could to shorten the session in order that my right hon. friend and his colleagues might be free to go to the world economic conference. But that is the extent to which courtesies from this side of the house are appreciated by hon. gentlemen opposite. The Prime Minister knows very well that, when he waited until the very end of the session to answer that question, and when he gave the answer he did, he was taking a step which made impossible any discussion. However, I say to my right hon. friend that if he thinks that a question which affects so largely the feelings of the people can be solved by such manoeuvres, to use a mild expression, I believe he will find he is greatly mistaken. If he really had desired to put an end for all time to titles in Canada, he could have adopted no more effective means than to flout as he has the opinion of this House of Commons which expresses the opinion of the country generally.
As I say, that was the position when parliament adjourned. What was the next thing that happened? To the surprise, I think of everyone, on the Friday night before New Year's, an announcement was made that the government or the Prime Minister had decided to recommend titles. I will read the statement which was given out to the country at that time by the Prime Minister. It is an important statement and I think it should appear fully upon the records. Having been asked by the press for a statement, the following was given by the Prime Minister on the evening of December 30:
As I intimated at the last session of parliament, the resolution passed in 1919 by the House of Commons, being one branch of parliament, is without validity in either restricting the royal prerogative or amending or repealing the existing law. It will readily be recalled that proceedings were taken many years ago against the publisher of the debates of the House of Commons in England, in which it was alleged that a well known citizen was libelled'.
The publisher sought to justify his action on the authority of a resolution passed by the House of Commons, but the courts decided that "the House of Commons is not the parliament, but only a coordinate and component part of parliament. The sovereign power can make and unmake laws; but the concurrence of the three legislative estates is necessary; the resolution of any one of them cannot alter the law or place anyone beyond its control. The proposition is therefore wholly untenable and abhorrent to the first principles of the constitution of England."	_
The resolution passed by the Canadian House of Commons in 1919 was transmitted to the Sovereign with great formality, but that could not give it validity, and I believe it is now generally realized that the resolution was * invalid for the purposes indicated by those who promoted and supported it.
Since that date Canadians have accepted honours from the heads of foreign states, and the government is of the opinion that the traditional custom of submitting recommendations to His Majesty for the bestowal of honours and awards should be resumed, and the Prime Minister has acted accordingly.

within the quotation. There, for the first time, the Prime Minister gives any reasons to substantiate the action of his government. Four reasons are mentioned. The first is that the resolution passed in 1919 by the House of Commons, being one branch of parliament, is without validity in either restricting the royal prerogative or amending or repealing the existing law. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the House of Commons and the House of Commons alone should direct the ministry with respect to all matters appertaining to the royal prerogative. It is not for the other house to direct the ministry regarding the prerogative. That is the duty of the House of Commons. It has always been so, or at any rate, for many years, it has been regarded by the House of Commons as one of its rights and privileges, and the House of Commons in Great Britain has been unwilling to admit that a statute is necessary to control the prerogative.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
On the contrary, it was
so declared in the House of Lords within this last month.

I had not intended going into the matter, but seeing that the Prime Minister has raised the point I may as well go somewhat farther. In 1870, the government of Mr. Gladstone had endeavoured to abolish by statute the system of purchase of commissions in the army, but . the bill was obstructed or defeated in the House of Lords. Mr. Gladstone thereupon advised the sovereign to cancel the royal warrant regulating the sale of commissions. Queen Victoria, recognizing that the ministry, which was responsible to the House of Commons,	was	the	source	from which	thesovereign should be directed in the matter of the exercise of the royal prerogative, acted upon the advice of Mr. Gladstone and issued a royal warrant cancelling the warrant regulating the purchase of commissions in the army,	and	the	system	of purchase	was
effectively disposed of in this way.
There is another case that came still later, in 1890. At that time a statute had been introduced by Lord Salisbury for the cession of Heligoland to Germany in consideration of Germany's having recognized the claims of Britain to Zanzibar. When the bill was before parliament Mr. Gladstone, ably seconded by Sir William Harcourt, took the view that the government, by making the treaty a subject of legislation, had abandoned the treatymaking prerogative of the crown. He pro-

ceeded to show that the prerogative of the crown, exercised by the ministers of the day, was subject to review by the House of Commons and by the House of Commons alone, whereas a bill required the sanction of the House of Lords. Mr. Gladstone pointed out that the commons, in countenancing such procedure and sharing its jurisdiction with the House of Lords, was halving a right which was peculiarly its own, namely, controlling the exercise of the royal prerogative. That position I think is the sound one-the position that the ministry is responsible to the House of Commons, and that the Commons should direct the ministry in this particular. That, I submit, is the true position to be taken with regard to the exercise of the royal prerogative.
The Prime Minister raises a very grave issue, an issue which is entirely new and which deprives this House of Commons of rights and privileges it ought zealously to maintain, when he states that, with respect to the exercise of the prerogative, the House of Commons must share that right with another house of this parliament. The control of the exercise of the royal prerogative in Canada is the peculiar right of this House of Commons, and I am amazed that one who is the leader of the House of Commons, deriving his authority from the House of Commons, should take any view to the contrary. If the House of Commons ceased to support him he would cease to be Prime Minister, notwithstanding all that the other house might seek to do for him, notwithstanding that every member in the other house might be a follower of his own. His power is entirely dependent upon the support he receives from this House of Commons. In the matter of the exercise of the royal prerogative, one of the most vital of the rights and privileges of the House of Commons is that of directing the ministry with respect to the manner in which it is to be exercised.
Take the next point. He says:
It will readily be recalled that proceedings were taken many years ago against the publisher of the debates of the House of Commons in England, in which it was alleged that a well known citizen was libelled.
I think I am right in saying that the case upon which the Prime Minister relies to support his position is that of Stockdale vs. Hansard-he says yes. Well, that case was decided in 1839, nearly one hundred years ago, and the Prime Minister tells us that it is in virtue of that decision given nearly a hundred years ago that he and his government to-day have taken the action they have. Now, what was that case? Stockdale was a publisher of

books and magazines, and one of his books had been referred to in a parliamentary report as being obscene, and on that ground he brought an action against Hansard Brothers, who were the publishers of the government reports, for having libelled his firm in giving publicity, in the way in which it was done, to this characterization of a particular book. Hansard Brothers set up the defence that they had been ordered by the House of Commons to publish its reports, and the courts very rightly held that an order of the House of Commons was not superior to the law of the land and that it could not protect Hansard Brothers in that libel action because a resolution of the House of Commons did not run beyond its own membership, and the law of the land was supreme. That is perfectly sound; certainly the law of the land is supreme. But that case, far from supporting my right hon. friend, does the very opposite. All that it does is to say that, outside of this House of Commons, no subject can plead a resolution of the House of Commons to protect him in an illegal act. What my right hon. friend overlooks however is the fact that a resolution passed by the House of Commons is binding upon those within the house, is binding upon the ministry, which is responsible to the House of Commons. It is not with respect to what lies outside of the House of Commons, but with respect to what takes place within the house, that the resolution has its force. The case of Stockdale vs. Hansard has no bearing on the question before us.
If my right hon. friend wanted constitutional authorities he would have been better advised to cite the case of Bradlaugh vs. Gosset, in which it was made perfectly clear that the courts could not control the Commons in the matter of their resolutions, and that the Commons could take action with respect to matters of concern to itself, which no court could interfere with. And that is what this House of Commons did when it passed the resolution of 1919. It was not trying to override the courts of the land or to circumscribe the royal prerogative by resolution. What the House of Commons was seeking to do was to restrict the powers of the ministry with respect to the advice to be given the sovereign in the exercise of the prerogative of conferring honours, and I say that in this regard the grounds which the Prime Minister has given in support of his position are untenable. At any rate, he should have waited until they were debated in the House of Commons before advancing them as a reason for the action which the government took.
What is the third reason he gives? He says:
I believe it is now generally realized that the resolution was invalid.
I take the opposite view. I think it is now recognized that the resolution was valid and that every hon. member had so believed for a period of ten or fifteen years. The governments of Sir Robert Borden, of the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen, and the late Liberal administration, and the last four parliaments as well, all believed that the resolution was valid.
The last ground is that Canadians have accepted honours from heads of foreign states which simply amounts to saying that two wrongs make a right. I agree that, if honours are not to be accepted by Canadians from the sovereign of our own country, certainly they should not be accepted from sovereigns of other countries. But the resolution of 1919 was not a controlling factor in that situation; it could not bind the ministry of the day with respect to foreign sovereigns and what they could do; the ministry had nothing to do with advising foreign sovereigns. To control a situation of the kind a statute would be necessary which would restrict the rights of Canadian subjects. But, in respect of advising our own sovereign, the ministry had full power and will continue to have it. In view of these considerations I say that the action of the Prime Minister was nothing short of an affront to the House of Commons; it was, to say the least, an act of discourtesy and I am not giving these words simply as my own. I have in my hand an editorial of the Winnipeg Tribune, which is a strong supporter of the administration.
