I was asked to explain.
Those are the words.

Yes, the Prime Minister was asked to explain, and I continued to ask him whether the purpose of introducing that measure was not to assert the right of the Commons to deal with matters of concern to themselves before taking up matters of concern to the crown. He, as I recall, replied that I, having been prime minister, ought to know the purpose as well as he did, seeing that this had been a custom for fifty years. May I point this out to my right hon. friend: not only has it been a custom for the last fifty years; it has been a custom from the reign of Queen Elizabeth, for the Commons to

assert its right to take up matters of concern to its members before dealing with matters of concern to the crown.
What is of more intimate concern to the Commons than the question of the prerogative of the crown and how the royal prerogative is to be exercised? Seeing that the governor General had summoned parliament and that the Prime Minister himself knows the tradition of the House of Commons with respect to the assertion of its right to deal with its own matters before taking up questions of concern to the crown, why did my right hon. friend take the step he did at that time? There can be only one of two explanations. One is that he must have anticipated that, if he did not take some action at that time, as soon as parliament met, the resolution of the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell) would come up, the whole question would be open for discussion, and that a course would be adopted similar to that which was proposed by the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan), namely, that a committee should be appointed to consider the matter and bring in a resolution and that the Prime Minister believed that, if any such committee were appointed, it would bring in a resolution praying His Majesty not to grant titles to Canadian subjects. If the Prime Minister knew or believed anything of that kind would occur, he was doubly wrong in taking the course he did, because he was going diametrically opposite to what in his heart of hearts he must have known was the feeling and wish of the House of Commons.
On the other hand, he may have feilt that if he could change the issue in some way, if he could bring it about that when the subject came up for discussion the position of the government would in consequence of their action be at stake, then, the question would be, not so much with respect to titles, as to whether or not hon. members opposite would retain their seats for the remainder of the present and possibly another session. In that way he may have thought the question of titles would be sidetracked and the real issue never faced. Here again if he entertained any such belief the Prime Minister was doubly wrong in the course he took. Those are two possible explanations; if there is any other, I hope the Prime Minister will give it to the House of Commons. The point that needs to be emphasized at the moment is that, in so far as the Prime Minister's action is concerned, we have to all intents and purposes been told that the question of the prerogative of the crown and the manner in which it is to be

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
exercised is of no concern to the House of Commons. That is one of the largest issues that can be raised. In taking the stand he did, he is entirely wrong. He has against him public opinion, as well, I believe, as hon. members of the house as a whole if they were free to express their own convictions.
I shall bring my remarks to a conclusion by making a reference-
Four hours.
My hon. friend says: "four hours".

Four hours and twelve
minutes.

If I were to
attempt to catalogue the sins of omission and commission of this government, I should have to talk for forty hours. I believe it is important at this time, to place before the house some of the reasons why not only hon. members on this side, but the country generally feel that the present ministry have lost all authority to continue to govern in this dominion.
Mr. Speaker, I would have concluded at this point, but for the fact that, for reasons best known to himself, the Prime Minister thought well on the eve of the reassembling of parliament to deliver in the city of Toronto an address about as offensive in the tone of its utterance and the extent of its misrepresentation, as any public speech could possibly be. I do not intend to let that Toronto speech pass without making some reference to it, even if it takes another hour to do so.
Let me read a few extracts from what the Prime Minister said, and in this connection I should like hon. members to consider the body that he was addressing. It was the annual banquet of the Federation of Conservative Young Canada Clubs of Ontario. We have in the Prime Minister's utterances the example which the present Prime Minister of Canada is setting young Canada of the manner in which public issues in this country are to be discussed. This is the way in which politics are to be kept upon a high plane in our country, and the manner in which national righteousness is to be upheld in the dominion. Let me read the first paragraph of the report as it appears in the Ottawa Journal of January 22, from Toronto by direct wire by Canadian Press. These are the words of the Prime Minister:
"The Conservative policy since confederation had been to keep faith with the best traditions of the past and to build a better and more
united Canada to pass along to posterity." the Prime Minister said. "The Liberal policy had been to seize upon every opportunity of suspicion and unrest, to tear down and destroy."
Hear, hear.

Yes, I expected some hon. gentlemen to say "hear, hear"; it is what I would expect from some of them. It was not what I would expect from many, and it did not come from many, I ask hon. gentlemen to listen to this:
Those who profess the Conservative faith art responsible for this great dominion. In time oi suspicion, doubt and unrest it has been to this great party that the people have always turned.
" Those who profess the Conservative faith are responsible for this great dominion." I cannot imagine that a more ungenerous, a more unchivalrous and a more untrue statement could possibly be made by any public man in Canada than what is expressed in those words. I should like to know whether in the Conservative party has been included all those early pioneers who settled this country, first of all those from France who settled in Quebec, and later those who settled this old province of Ontario. I should like to know whether in the Conservative party of Canada has been included all those who pioneered in the great west and out on the Pacific slope. I should like to know whether in the Conservative party has been included all those who sought in one way and another to serve their country in these halls of parliament. If it has not been so, the statement of the Prime Minister is as untrue as it is unchivalrous and ungenerous. Yet these are the words which he addressed to the youth of the Conservative party; this is the example he set for them in discussing the public issues of the day. To-night I am not going even to attempt to refer to what has been done in this country by great men of both political parties, but I will say that, so far as the upbuilding of Canada is concerned, any man who is patriotic in the true sense of the word will be only too ready to share with men of all political parties the praise that is to be given to those who have taken part in this great work.
Now what is the next statement, Mr. Speaker? It has reference to preferences. Here is what the Prime Minister is reported to have said to the young men who are coming on:	"For thirty-five years the
country laboured to undo the wrong done by the Liberal party in regard to preferential tariffs and reciprocal trade within the empire," he declared, recalling Laurier's assertion in
51	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
London that " what we give we give you freely," and without hope of return. " In 1932 this situation was rectified, and preferential, reciprocal trading agreements with all parts of the empire were negotiated."
For thirty-five years, the Prime Minister said, this parliament laboured to undo the wrong done by the parliament of Canada in regard to preferential tariffs.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not this parliament.

To undo the wrong done by the Liberal party in regard to preferential tariffs. It was parliament that enacted the preference. In making this statement apparently the Prime Minister forgets that Sir Robert Borden, as leader of the Conservative party, held office in this country for many years and that Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, as leader of a Conservative administration, also held office in Canada for some considerable time. During all that period of time when the Conservatives were in power, the British preferences introduced by Sir Wilfrid Laurier remained on the statute books to all intents and purposes unchanged. Yet the Prime Minister tells these young men, who are to be trained in accuracy and truth in discussing public matters, that for thirty-five yeare the country has laboured to undo the wrong done by the Liberal party in regard to empire preferential tariffs.
What is the fact with regard to preferential tariffs? When Sir Wilfrid Laurier introduced the preferences he did so because he believed that by giving a preference to Great Britain he would encourage trade both ways across the Atlantic; that, by giving a preference in our markets to some British goods, a greater demand would be created in Britain for the products of our farms, fields, forests and mines, and that a larger amount of trade would pass between this country and the old land, also that consumers in Canada generally would benefit. What was the result? The Prime Minister tells us to-day that the way to find out whether or not a country is prosperous is to look at its balance of trade. What is the result when we look at the balance of trade over that period? Taking it from the time the British preference was introduced down to the time of the United Kingdom-Canada agreement, there was a favourable balance of trade so far as Canada was concerned every year. This is the wrong that the Prime Minister says the Conservative party of Canada has been trying to undo. In those thirty-four fiscal years, the total of Canada's favourable balance of trade with the United Kingdom amounted to $5,978,000,000.

That was the result of the British preference as introduced by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and this benefit to Canada's trade is the great wrong which the Conservative party has sought to undo by means of this United Kingdom-Canada agreement.
But that, Mr. Speaker, was not the only subject on which the right hon. gentleman touched. He had a word to say about the depression, and here I think he was running pretty true to form. His utterances reminded me, as I think perhaps I will be able to show him, of some of the things he said in the last campaign. What do you imagine the present Prime Minister said to these young men, Mr. Speaker, of the attitude of his political opponents towards the existing depression. Here are his words:
"And while those of Conservative faith have been working with high courage and unstinted effort to bring an even keel, what do we find' on the Liberal side," he asked. "We find unrest capitalized, suspicion capitalized, distrust sown, efforts everywhere to tear down the faith of the people by teaching strange doctrines and the worship of stranger gods. They have indulged in a campaign of reckless, harsh, unending criticism, fundamentally directed against our basic institutions and the foundations on which they are built."
I do not know, Mr. Speaker, of any government that has ever been given quite as free a hand in carrying out its policies as has the present administration. I do not believe there has been a leader of an opposition at any time in this parliament or any other parliament who has been more generous to his opponents than I have been in the matter of criticism in these trying times. If any complaint has been made against me by my own friends, it has been that I have not spent more time in condemning the government in all parts of the country. But I have recognized the difficulties with which they have had to contend, and I have felt that the country would feel it was reasonable to allow the ministry as free a hand as possible, though in this parliament I have not hesitated to say quite frankly what I thought when I believed their policies were doing more harm than good and when I felt they were exceeding all rights, even under the pretence of their doing so in order to meet an emergency. When the Prime Minister uses language like this, I am obliged to recall to him some of his own words, in order that the young men of the country may see it is the sort of thing he is accustomed to say. He said that the Liberal party had been seeking to capitalize unrest and suspicion, to sow distrust and to tear down the faith of our people. Listen to this, Mr. Speaker:

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
Here is what the same gentleman said in an address to the electors of this country in the city of Winnipeg on the -occasion of his opening a great political campaign the result of which was to bring him into office. The right hon. gentleman accuses the Liberal party of seeking to tear down the faith of the people. Let me read some of his statements; first in reference to the government of the day:
This group of mercenaries holding office by sham and subterfuge, look upon them as treacherous to you, self-confessed, deserving of your passionate condemnation.
Then, speaking at Regina:
Now we have unemployment, people walking our streets, men and women hungry. We have all these things in this great rich country.
-Of course there is no effort in those expressions to capitalize unrest and sow dis-distrust! Then, listen to this:
They play with the lives of men and women. What for? Do they realize there are lives that they are playing with, food for wives and children, hunger. Nine years of wasted effort before the great betrayal. It did not take Judas that long.
No capitalizing of unrest in that; no seeking to raise suspicions; no sowing of the seeds of distrust; no effort to tear down the faith of the people in their institutions or their leaders in expressions like that-no.
Referring to myself, he said:
However blind he may be to your future and deaf to your present needs surely he cannot stop his ears with smug complacence and self-esteem, to the cry that carries across the nation, the cry of the destitute and hungry, the cry of mothers and fathers and little children who call to us as Christians and as Canadians to heal their pain.
No sowing of distrust or suspicion or capitalizing of unrest in these words. But by way of recognition of the moderate attitude which his political opponents have taken toward him and his administration, he tells the young Conservatives of this country that it is in language such -as this they are to learn to speak of their political opponents. I shall say no more upon that subject. I submit however, that something better than that might have found expression from the lips of one who has been holding and still holds the office of Prime Minister in Canada. Something better than that should have been forthcoming and was due the type of audience the Prime Minister was addressing.
The next subject to which the Prime Minister referred was that of the railways. For some reason or another he keeps reverting to the question of railways, always Striving to make it appear that the railway problem in Canada
to-day is due exclusively to the policies of the Liberal party, and that anything the Conservative party has done is in no way responsible for railway difficulties. In regard to the railways the Prime Minister said:
The Conservative policy has been constructive and it left a legacy of a united dominion with one transcontinental railway binding its scattered provinces together. The Liberal party left a legacy of two transcontinental railways in addition to the one already in existence, and impaired our financial resources for generations to come that two might exist in order to destroy all three.
Can you believe that, Mr. Speaker? That is an exact quotation from a press report. The statement is that, first of all, the Liberal party constructed an additional two transcontinental roads, and did so why? They did it, the Prime Minister says, so that the two might exist in order to destroy all three! To continue the right hon. gentleman's remarks:
To-day we have $1,000,000,000 of indirect debt to bear witness to their shortsightedness, costing us $1,500,000 a week in interest charges alone.
Legacy of debt, perpetual deficits and duplication of railway facilities left by the Liberals when they stepped down from power.
No doubt the railways to which my right hon. friend referred were the National Transcontinental and Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk system which has been taken into the present Canadian National Railway system, the Intercolonial and the Canadian Pacific Railway. May I remind the right hon. gentleman to begin with, that the Intercolonial and the Grand Trunk railway were constructed before the Canadian Pacific railway had been thought of. The Prim-e Minister knows that the construction of the National Transcontinental and Grand Trunk Pacific was the subject of discussion, the main issue in fact, in two- general elections. One party alone did not have to do with that matter. The Canadian people as a whole approved of the construction of that railway. As my hon. friends well know, they approved of it in two general elections.
Nonsense.

May I remind the hon. members who have interrupted that when they criticize the Liberal party for having constructed the transcontinental road, which is now government owned, they must remember that the leader of the Conservative party took issue with the Liberal government when it proposed to have part of the transcontinental system-the Grand Trunk Pacific- controlled by a private corporation, and took
56	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
the position that the entire transcontinental road ought to be government owned. On May 26, 1904, Sir Robert Borden, leader of the Conservative party, moved a resolution which, while differing from the proposal of the Laurier government, was equally a proposal for a second transcontinental railway. Let me read Sir Robert Borden's motion as it appears in Hansard of May 26, 1904:
The house is of opinion that _ instead of ratifying the proposed agreements it would be more in the public interest that the dominion should assume the whole obligation necessary for extending across the continent the. present government system of railways thereby completing a transcontinental railway from the Atlantic to the Pacific entirely owned by and under the control of the people of Canada.
I wonder how it is that the Conservative party is to share no responsibility for the construction of a second transcontinental railway when that is the policy enunciated in this house and upon which it based its claim to power in a general election.
Then, what about the Canadian Northern Railway? That railway was begun as a local underbaking in the province of Manitoba, and extended over the prairies. The Canadian Northern management came to the Liberal administration and asked for a guarantee of a loan of $35,000,000 to enable them to connect their western lines with the centres in the east. That guarantee was given by the Liberal administration very largely in order to help the farmers of western Canada. The Liberal administration was also asked for a guarantee of a loan to make possible the extension of the road to the Pacific ocean. That request, however, the Liberal government refused; but the application was granted later by a Conservative government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: By a provincial government.
What about the $75,000,000?

What are the facts in connection with the actual construction of the mileage of the Canadian Northern? The annual report of the Department of Railways and Canals shows that up to the year 1911 there were 4,840 miles of operated line. In 1914 there were 6,542 miles and in 1920 there were 9,742. In other words, the largest part of the Canadian Northern system was built during the term of office of the Conservative administration, yet the Prime Minister states we have to thank the Liberal party for all the roads in existence save the Canadian Pacific. May I go a step further and remind my hon. friend about some of his own statements. He himself spoke, I do not know

whether it was for four hours, but I think it was about that length of time, on this very matter, vehemently condemning his own party, the Conservative party, not the Liberal party, when in 1914 it guaranteed a $45,000,000 loan for the completion of the Canadian Northern as a third transcontinental. Though my hon. friend says, "hear, hear'' to my remarks, he told the Young Conservatives of Toronto that it was the Liberals they had ito thank for these railways.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

May I come to another phase? My hon. friend speaks of deficits and the like. What did he himself say in this very parliament in claiming credit for the Canadian National once it had got into good running order under years of Liberal administration? Both he and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) tried to claim for the Conservative party the paternity of this second transcontinental road. Let me read the Prime Minister's own words spoken in this house on June 8, 1928:
The consolidation of these roads took place first under the Union government and later under the Conservative administration. The consolidation could not be carried into effect until the judgment of the privy council was delivered, and that judgment was not delivered until after the Conservative administration had been defeated. But the consolidation as such, the framework, the skeleton and the statutes were prepared before the present government took office.	.
That was when the Liberal party were making a success of the Canadian National and the present Prime Minister was seeking to claim the credit for it. What did the Minister of Justice say about the national railway? He did not give credit to his present deskmate, the Prime Minister, but he did give credit to another leader of the Conservative party, and in very emphatic terms. Speaking in this house on March 7, 1929, he said:
The National Railway system in this country constitutes a lasting monument-
Not to the Liberal party, but a lasting monument:
-to the ability and statesmanship and determination of a single man-
Not the present Prime Minister:

a member of a former Conservative government, and subsequently Prime Minister of that government. It is to his ability and foresight, to his statesmanship and determination that the people of Canada are indebted for this wonderful system of National railways.
I might quote at some length to show how the deficits on these roads have mounted up

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
to what they are. I wonder if the Prime Minister has forgotten what was done by a Conservative administration with respect to the stock of the Canadian Northern, how, notwithstanding the report of the Drayton-Acworth commission that the stock of the Canadian Northern was of no value, or in the actual words of the report:
The shareholders of the company have no equity either on the ground of cash put in, or on the ground of physical reproduction cost, or on the ground of the saleable value of their property as a going concern.
-how, notwithstanding that that report was before them, a Conservative government gave a value of $10,000,000 to that valueless stock, thereby adding that much to the debt of this country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Not a government but a
commission.
It was a Conservative government that agreed to pay the money.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It was an arbitration by
a commission.

I could mention other matters which perhaps the Prime Minister has forgotten. It was the government of 1917, not a Liberal government, that brought down the Canadian Northern railway acquisition bill. When these roads and the Grand Trunk were in a state of bankruptcy it was a Conservative government which, instead of permitting them to go into the hands of a receiver, took over the whole obligations, paid out money and incurred fresh liabilities in taking over these roads and their debts, and making them part of the debt of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is what I opposed.

The Prime
Minister says he opposed it, and yet he tells the Young Conservatives in Toronto that the Liberal party was responsible for all these obligations.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I shall not at
the moment take up the time of the house by recalling what was given to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in land grants and in money, exemptions from taxation, and the rest of it. If I wanted to, I think I could show how a very considerable part of our debt has been due to what was given by the Conservative government to the Canadian Pacific Railway.
But there is one order in council to which I wish to refer before I conclude, and that
is a new railway guarantee given by the present government since this house prorogued last session. I have in my hand a copy of an order in council giving a guarantee to the banks of their loan of $60,000,000 to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The loan was made by the banks I believe in midsummer, or an undertaking was given I understand at that time that the loan would be made. On November 29 the government formally by order in council guaranteed the banks to the extent of $60,000,000 in this matter, and Mr. Speaker, this was done under the Unemployment Relief Act. Again this is for the relief of the unemployed. This is the kind of thing that I have been taking exception to all afternoon, the guaranteeing and expending of public moneys for the purpose of assisting corporations, and then allowing it to be understood by the public that these millions upon millions are being spent in order to help unemployed workers in different parts of the country.
I should like to know why the Prime Minister kept this order secret for so long a time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He did not. It was issued on November 29 when it was passed, and a copy of it was sent to the right hon. gentleman by myself.

In the early
part of the summer word was current all over the country that the government was going to support the banks in their loan to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The order in council itself sets out the reasons for it.

I have the order in council, and as my hon. friend says, and as I expected he would say, he sent me a copy. It is the only copy of an order in council he has sent to me during the time I have been leader of the opposition. The order in council was passed on November 29, and a copy of it was sent to me a few days afterwards, probably because my hon. friend had seen that a month or so before, when it was current rumour that the order had been passed, I had stated that I did not know whether the order in council had been passed or not, but that if it had been passed I thought parliament should at least have been consulted before any guarantee of such an amount should be given to any corporation. The Prime Minister was evidently anxious that I should see that the order in council had not been passed at the time I had been speaking. But the significant thing is that
5S	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
the banks had got their undertaking months before. Why was the credit of this country promised to the banks? They had made their loans under the guarantee of the government, and on the understanding that the government was going to support them, and I cannot understand why the passing of this order in council should have been delayed until November 29. The country's credit had evidently been pledged on the word of the Prime Minister, and without any order in council. Before the session is over we shall doubtless find out.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The order in council shows the reason why.
Mr. MACKENZIE KIN'G: The reasons as I have read them are not very conclusive. It was clear at the time they sought it, that the railways knew where the money was coming from and that the government was going to be back of the loans made by the banks. What I do take exception to is that, in these matters which involve an increase in what the Prime Minister has described as a colossal public debt already arising from the railways, we in this House of Commons should be made responsible for another guarantee of $60,000,000 to a railway, and not have an opportunity of even having our voices heard. That is the ground upon which I take exception. This is only one of a large number of orders in council of a similar kind relating to the guaranteeing of millions of dollars of the country's money, millions to guarantee the banks on account of wheat, millions to support railway corporations and assist other corporations, and yet in all of these things the House of Commons, which is responsible to the people for the expenditure of public money and is supposed to exercise some control over it has not had any voice at all and knew very little and in some instances nothing at all about the transactions themselves. The Prime Minister will probably say that the house was not in session when it was necessary to issue the orders. May I say to the Prime Minister that he is able to anticipate most needs before parliament prorogues and that he is always at liberty to call the house into session. If there is a necessity to make a guarantee of $60,000,000 to a railway corporation or to banks that have loaned that amount, that is ground in itself sufficient for bringing the House of Commons together to discuss the matter. We have had special sessions and there is no reason why the government should not in this matter as in many others have consulted the House of Commons.
This enables me to stress the point I sought to bring out with emphasis this afternoon, namely, that in all its major acts this

government has for the most part ignored the House of Commons. We are treated as though we were here simply for the purpose of registering the will of the government, and, as the Prime Minister himself has said, being a sort of rubber stamp.
Mr, BENNETT: What do you mean by that?

Not only has the House of Commons grounds for having lost confidence in the government, but the government no longer enjoys the confidence of the people. As I said at the beginning of my remarks this afternoon, this lack of confidence of the people in this government has been made abundantly clear by the way in which the people have spoken at every opportunity they have had in by-elections during the last couple of years whether the election has been held in the maritime provinces, in Quebec, in Ontario or in the west. The government's policies have not brought about the improvement in conditions which the government said would come under them. Conditions have become worse instead of better. The government has failed to bring forth any real policy on agriculture * it has failed to bring forth any real policy on finance and monetary matters; it has failed to bring forth any policy on labour matters. It has had no policy except one of restriction in matters of trade. In all these things and in many others, it has been deplorably deficient.
With respect to matters in which this House of Commons is vitally interested in preserving its own rights and privileges, andi thereby protecting the people in their rights, the government has been more than indifferent. It has forfeited every right to continue longer in office. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I beg to move an amendment to the address which I believe to be demanded by the people in consequence of the hopeless way in which the government has carried on the administration of the country's affairs during the last three and a half years. It affords the only means of giving expression to their views, the only means whereby the country can expect the change of policies needed in order to get Canada out of this prolonged depression and again on the path to prosperity. The amendment is seconded by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), and is as follows:
That the following be added' to the motion: "We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that Your Excellency's present advisers do not possess the confidence of the country."

The Address-Mr. Bennett

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to
something over four hours of effort on the part of the right hon. leader of the opposition * (Mr. Mackenzie King) one would conclude that we are living in the days of abounding prosperity and that this was a debating society met together for the purpose of having a little friendly discussion. There has been nothing to indicate that the country has been in the throes of the greatest depression of history; nothing to indicate by any stretch of the imagination that we have been passing through the greatest Catastrophe of history. Comparisons have been .instituted of the trade of 1927, 1928 and 1929 with the trade of the most depressing years of which the world has had a record. Incomparable things have been compared, and it has been sought to have the house believe that the conclusion to be drawn from these comparisons constitute good reasons why this government should lose the confidence of the house.
May I direct attention to the fact that Mr. Ramsay MacDonald at the opening of the world economic conference pointed out that during the period of depression the world's trade had decreased to one-third of what it was before the depression began. Was there anything this afternoon that would indicate there had been a world depression in trade? Was there anything from which one could conclude there was anything other than a passing wave of depression in some remote parts of the world with which Canada had no connection? The other day we had the authority for the statement that the world's trade had fallen to $25,000,000,000, although somewhat improved over what it was a few years ago, while previously it had been $69,000,000,000; therefore the fall has been from $69,000,000,000 to $25,000,000,000. The total of the world's commerce for the last twelve months, reckoned from November, was thirty-six per cent of what it was before the depression began. When I say to my fellow Canadians that their country has done just as well as if not a little better than the average in that our trade has remained at least thirty-six per cent of what it was before the depression, I speak but the simple truth. Yet during all of this afternoon there was not a single indication that the Dominion of Canada had been affected by the world depression. Is that fair, especially in view of the declaration of fairness and righteousness to which we have just listened? Is it exactly what we would expect from such a professor of righteousness? We would hardly expect the author of a new prayer to do a thing such as
that. It is a little difficult to think that one who had played with the most solemn things of life by creating a new prayer, especially a member of the House of Commons, would be for one moment guilty of discussing the world's condition without reference to the fact that Canada also had been affected. It is an amazing story. I desire the House of Commons to know that we have passed through a depression and that this story of Canadian trade to which we have listened to-day is the story of all countries of the world, only that our country has been a little better off than most of them.
This afternoon and this evening I was reminded of those speeches to which we used to listen when hon. gentlemen opposite sat upon this side of the Speaker and references to the condition of the country were made by the opposition. We were told that this was the blue ruin tale of Tories. Do you recall them? Do you recall the wailing of Jeremiah which was passed on to the people of this country?
The whisper of death.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman should know of the whisper of death. Attacks have been made upon the accuracy of statistics which have been prepared without reference to governments by those who at Geneva and in meetings of the League of Nations have been referred to as the foremost in the science of statistics. Mr. Coats did not consult any member of the government in the preparation of his statistics. The figures of unemployment which were given and to which I shall refer to-morrow were arrived at from returns made by companies and organizations which reported to the government just as they reported in the days when the right hon. gentleman sat to the right of the Speaker. Do you think that by such references as these you improve conditions in Canada? Do you think you do not bring upon yourself condemnation? Do you think men will not say that your one stock in trade is an endeavour to tear down? Do you think it is not an appeal to prejudice and passion? Apart from creating a new prayer, apart from the attacks which have been made upon responsible officials, overlooking the fact that the country has passed through the direst years of which we have any record; apart from all this, tell me what purpose is served by endeavouring to paint, in blacker hues than they appear, the conditions of your native country? What purpose is there in endeavouring to make it appear that things are darker than they actually are? Why endeavour to discourage the hope and confidence of the
The Address-Mr. Bennett

people? Why endeavour to tell a story which is blacker than the real conditions that prevail in the country?
Although in doing so I shall depart from my usual custom, I will take some little time to deal with every point that has been raised to-day, and I will defy the right hon. gentleman, or anyone else who may follow after him, to contend, in the light of the real facts in this country, as recorded by historians and statisticians not only in Canada but elsewhere, that this dominion has not made progress towards prosperity and a return to better days, greater than has been made in most other countries in the world. When I hear held up to high praise, the attitude taken by the president of the great republic to the south of us, whom I see exercising almost autocratic powers under authority from congress, I realize the puny powers which we possess under the Relief Act. I find that on one hand approval is given when someone else exercises authority, while on the other hand there is denunciation when we endeavour to exercise similar authority. If the exercise of executive authority under powers conferred by act of congress is a salutary and good thing for the nation in which such authority is exercised, why does it, when it is north of the forty-ninth parallel, cease to be good when similar actions have been taken by the executive in this country, with results that are comparable in every respect?
To those in this house who entertain other views I commend the reading of an article that appeared recently in the Saturday Evening Post, "North of the N.R.A.", written by Mr. Marcosson, whom I did not see and who did not consult me in any way with respect to it. There hon. gentlemen will find his record, after investigation, of the way in which this dominion, with ten and a half millions and with limited financial resources, cribbed, cabinned and confined financially, has been able to meet the storm of the depression as compared with a nation of one hundred and twenty-five millions south of the forty-ninth parallel, with the Nit.A. In order that ample opportunity may be afforded hon. gentlemen to study that record, I now move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Bennett the house adjourned at 10.45 p.m.
Tuesday, January 30, 1934
